newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - NZ FEC chair critical of Peters' answers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NZ FEC chair critical of Peters' answers.

text.p: Finance and Expenditure committee chairman Tony Ryall on Thursday criticised as evasive New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters' answers to questions before the committee.

"I just wish the person, the people being examined would be a little bit more forthcoming than they are. I think in this last episode (with Peters) I don't think that many of the questions that were asked were answered," Ryall said in an interview with Reuters.

Peters became Treasurer in the coalition government three months ago. He appeared before the powerful committee for the first time last week at the examination of the Budget Policy Statement (BPS) which sets out the government's broad fiscal plans.
Ryall said as chairman of the parliamentary committee he had no real powers to demand a more complete answer.
The examination of the BPS would also be improved if the executive and the committee could enter into more dialogue, he said.
Ryall said some provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility Act (FRA), introduced by the previous conservative National government, needed to be changed.
The FRA sets out the government's reporting obligations including the timing of the BPS.
"We have had the FRA for two or three years and it is timely to review its effectiveness," Ryall said.
He said now the Budget was being prepared earlier, the timing of the BPS, due by March 31, was getting out of step.
The committee could recommend refinements to the FRA, and he would like to see the BPS tabled in January.
"Changing the timing of the BPS does not require an amendment. I think we would be pretty reluctant to amend the Act."
He said the committee also needed to consider whether its deliberations had any impact on the writing of the Budget.

"I'm not sure it does. It would be nice to be pleasantly surprised. But the benefit of it is that you do have parliamentary scrutiny in a more focused way. And it also brings the Treasurer to account...before senior parliamentary colleagues in a way the parliamentary debating process doesn't." Ryall said he would like to involve private sector people
more to advise and comment to the committee.

"In this latest budget policy round and the economic projections comment from (Reserve Bank governor) Dr Don Brash, I think there might have been some benefit in us talking to private sector economists before we talked to (him) to enhance and focus our questioning."
Ryall said the committee was likely to continue the independent reputation it gained under former chairman Max Bradford.
"It is a committee made up of more senior members of parliament and as such it is always going to try and follow an independent line."
He said the membership of the committee was a "quite private enterprise group of people".
Apart from Alliance MP John Wright, all of its members supported the economic reforms of the past 12 years.
During 1997 Ryall would like to improve scrutiny of non-core government departments to help reduce waste. He said he would also like to see changes to the financial reviews of departments.
"They are a complete and utter waste of time, not just superficial but also political."

He said a subcommittee of the Government Administration and finance committees should look at incorporating standard questionnaires into departments' annual reports which could be the new basis for financial reviews.
